eOptShrinkQ: Near-Lossless KV Cache Compression Through Optimal Spectral Denoising and Quantization

Pei-Chun Su ††thanks: Corresponding author: pei-chun.su@yale.edu Affiliation: Department of Applied and Computational Mathematics, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
Abstract

We show that the key-value (KV) cache in transformer attention heads admits a natural decomposition into a low-rank shared context component and a full-rank per-token residual, well described by the spiked random matrix model. This observation leads to eOptShrinkQ, a two-stage compression pipeline: optimal singular value shrinkage (eOptShrink) automatically extracts the shared structure, and the residual—which satisfies the thin shell property with delocalized coordinates—is quantized by TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2025), a recently proposed per-vector scalar quantizer with near-optimal distortion guarantees. By restoring the isotropy that scalar quantization assumes, spectral denoising eliminates the need for both outlier handling and dedicated inner product bias correction, freeing those bits for improved reconstruction.

The theoretical grounding in random matrix theory provides three guarantees: automatic rank selection via the BBP phase transition, provably near-zero inner product bias on the residual, and coordinate delocalization ensuring near-optimal quantization distortion. Experimentally, we validate eOptShrinkQ on Llama-3.1-8B and Ministral-8B across three levels: per-head MSE and inner product fidelity, where eOptShrinkQ saves nearly one bit per entry over TurboQuant at equivalent quality; end-to-end on LongBench (16 tasks), where eOptShrinkQ at ∼\sim2.2 bits per entry outperforms TurboQuant at 3.0 bits; and multi-needle retrieval, where eOptShrinkQ at 2.2 bits closely matches or exceeds uncompressed FP16, suggesting that spectral denoising can act as a beneficial regularizer for retrieval-intensive tasks.

1 Introduction

The KV cache bottleneck.

The key-value (KV) cache is a critical memory bottleneck in autoregressive inference with large language models (LLMs). For a model with LL layers, hh attention heads, model dimension dmodeld_{\text{model}}, head dimension d=dmodel/hd=d_{\text{model}}/h, and context length TT, the KV cache stores 2​L​h​T​d2LhTd entries in half-precision, consuming gigabytes of GPU memory at long context lengths. Reducing this footprint through quantization has emerged as a practical necessity for long-context deployment. Since attention scores are computed as inner products ⟨q,k⟩/d\langle q,k\rangle/\sqrt{d}, the fidelity of these inner products after compression directly determines output quality—making inner product (IP) bias and variance the key metrics for KV cache quantization.

Per-vector scalar quantization.

Recent work has made remarkable progress on per-vector quantization of high-dimensional vectors. TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2025) achieves near-optimal distortion rates by compressing each key or value vector independently: a random orthogonal rotation isotropizes the vector, after which per-coordinate Lloyd-Max scalar quantization (Lloyd, 1982; Max, 1960) achieves near-optimal MSE for the resulting approximately Gaussian coordinates. At 3.5 bits per entry, TurboQuant matches full-precision performance on LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct—a strong baseline that we adopt as our downstream quantizer.

However, per-vector methods treat each vector independently, ignoring the structured nature of the KV cache. Within an attention head, a block of nn consecutive key or value vectors S~∈ℝn×d\widetilde{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} is not a collection of independent random vectors—it contains a low-rank component reflecting shared structure across tokens. This shared structure means the quantizer’s theoretical assumptions (isotropy on the unit sphere) are not fully satisfied, leading to inner product bias. TurboQuant’s QJL correction addresses this at the cost of one bit per coordinate; our approach instead removes the structure before quantization, restoring the isotropy that makes per-vector quantization optimal.

KV cache blocks as spiked random matrices.

We argue that the spectral structure of KV cache blocks is naturally described by the spiked matrix model from random matrix theory (Baik et al., 2005; Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi, 2012). Consider how keys are generated in a single attention head: for token tt with hidden state ht∈ℝdmodelh_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}, the key vector is s~t=RoPE​(ht​WK,t)∈ℝd\widetilde{s}_{t}=\text{RoPE}(h_{t}W_{K},t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where WK∈ℝdmodel×dW_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d} is the learned key projection and RoPE applies a position-dependent rotation. A block of nn consecutive key vectors (the block size) forms the rows of S~∈ℝn×d\widetilde{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}.

Each hidden state hth_{t} carries two types of information: (1) local context h¯t\bar{h}_{t}—the component that lies in a low-dimensional subspace shared by neighboring tokens within the block, reflecting common topic, discourse structure, and semantic context, and (2) token-specific content ϵt\epsilon_{t}—the unique semantic contribution of that particular token. Writing ht=h¯t+ϵth_{t}=\bar{h}_{t}+\epsilon_{t}, each row of the key block decomposes as:

S~[t,:]=R⁡(t)⋅h¯t​WK⏟S[t,:]+R⁡(t)⋅ϵt​WK⏟Z[t,:],\widetilde{S}[t,:]=\underbrace{R(t)\cdot\bar{h}_{t}W_{K}}_{S[t,:]}+\underbrace{R(t)\cdot\epsilon_{t}W_{K}}_{Z[t,:]}, (1)

where R⁡(t)R(t) is the orthogonal RoPE rotation at position tt. This gives the spiked model S~=S+Z\widetilde{S}=S+Z, where the tt-th row of the signal matrix is S[t,:]=R(t)⋅h¯tWKS[t,:]=R(t)\cdot\bar{h}_{t}W_{K} and the tt-th row of the residual is Z[t,:]=R(t)⋅ϵtWKZ[t,:]=R(t)\cdot\epsilon_{t}W_{K}. The signal SS is low-rank because the local context vectors {h¯t}t=1n\{\bar{h}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{n} span a low-dimensional subspace of ℝdmodel\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}—the rank rr reflects how many independent contextual directions are present within the block. Both WKW_{K} (a deterministic learned projection) and R⁡(t)R(t) (an orthogonal rotation) are applied identically to h¯t\bar{h}_{t} and ϵt\epsilon_{t}. Since deterministic linear transformations preserve the independence of their inputs, SS and ZZ are independent whenever h¯t⟂ϵt\bar{h}_{t}\perp\epsilon_{t}—regardless of WKW_{K} or R⁡(t)R(t).

  • •

    The signal S=∑i=1rdi​𝐮i​𝐯i⊤S=\sum_{i=1}^{r}d_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{\top} is low-rank because the local context vectors {h¯t}\{\bar{h}_{t}\} span a low-dimensional subspace when projected into head space by WKW_{K}. The right singular vectors 𝐯i∈ℝd\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} encode the principal directions of this local subspace—directions that the model has learned to use for attention matching. The left singular vectors 𝐮i∈ℝn\mathbf{u}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} describe how each token’s participation in these shared directions varies across the block; for keys, RoPE imposes smooth positional modulation on 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_{i}, which predicts that consecutive tokens should share stronger low-rank structure than randomly ordered tokens. Because SS is low-rank, it can be stored compactly via its SVD factors rather than redundantly encoded into every row by a per-vector quantizer.

  • •

    The residual Z∈ℝn×dZ\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} arises from the per-token variations ϵt\epsilon_{t} projected into head space by WKW_{K}. We emphasize that ZZ is not noise in the information-theoretic sense: it carries the token-specific information essential for distinguishing individual vectors during attention. However, from the perspective of the spiked model, ZZ plays the role of the “noise” matrix because it lacks the low-rank structure that can be efficiently compressed via SVD. The residual exhibits a separable covariance structure Z=A1/2​X​B1/2Z=A^{1/2}XB^{1/2} (Yang, 2019; Ding and Yang, 2021), where X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} has independent entries representing the truly token-specific and dimension-specific variation, A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} captures temporal dependence among the per-token variations (nearby tokens may carry related but distinct unique information due to local context), and B∈ℝd×dB\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} captures coordinate-wise covariance of the per-token variations in head space.

The independence of SS and ZZ follows from the independence of their sources: SS is driven by the local context h¯t\bar{h}_{t} and ZZ by the per-token variations ϵt\epsilon_{t}, with h¯t⟂ϵt\bar{h}_{t}\perp\epsilon_{t}. As established above, WKW_{K} and R⁡(t)R(t) are deterministic transformations that preserve this independence. We validate the spiked model empirically in Section 4.1, where the predicted spectral behavior (outlier eigenvalues, bulk distribution, and phase transition) closely matches observed KV cache spectra across layers and heads.

For value vectors, the same decomposition applies with WVW_{V} replacing WKW_{K} and no RoPE rotation: S~[t,:]=h¯tWV+ϵtWV\widetilde{S}[t,:]=\bar{h}_{t}W_{V}+\epsilon_{t}W_{V}. The shared structure SS is still present (tokens in a block share semantic context), and the per-token component ZZ captures what each token contributes to the attention output.

In the spiked model, a phase transition occurs at a critical strength α\alpha (Baik et al., 2005): shared components with di>αd_{i}>\alpha produce outlier singular values that separate from the bulk spectrum and are recoverable, while weaker components with di≤αd_{i}\leq\alpha are entangled with the token-specific part and cannot be separated by any method. The threshold α\alpha depends on the full covariance structure through AA and BB, not just the variance of ZZ—this is why the colored noise extension of optimal shrinkage is essential.

Optimal shrinkage for structured denoising.

The classical approach to recovering SS from S~\widetilde{S} via truncated SVD is suboptimal: hard thresholding discards weak-but-detectable signals and retains noise-inflated singular values. Optimal singular value shrinkage (Donoho and Gavish, 2013; Donoho et al., 2018; Nadakuditi, 2014) addresses both issues by computing the Frobenius-norm-optimal correction to each singular value, accounting for the aspect ratio and noise distribution. In our prior work (Su and Wu, 2025), we developed eOptShrink, which extends the OptShrink framework (Nadakuditi, 2014) to handle non-square matrices and colored noise with separable covariance—both essential for KV cache blocks where n≠dn\neq d and the noise statistics are non-white. eOptShrink additionally provides fully data-driven rank estimation via the BBP phase transition threshold, without requiring knowledge of the noise covariance structure.

The optimal shrinkage framework under white noise (TRAD) has found wide applications, including diffusion MRI denoising (Veraart et al., 2016), fetal electrocardiogram (fECG) extraction from trans-abdominal maternal ECG (Su et al., 2019), seismic data enhancement (Anvari et al., 2018), and stimulation artifact removal from intracranial EEG (Alagapan et al., 2019). In our prior work (Su and Wu, 2025), we developed eOptShrink to handle the more realistic setting of colored noise with separable covariance. There, the motivating application was fECG extraction, where the decomposition S~=S+Z\widetilde{S}=S+Z separates the dominant maternal ECG (SS) from the fetal ECG (ZZ)—two physiologically independent signals measured through the same electrode array. Crucially, the “noise” ZZ in that setting is itself a clinically important signal with non-white statistics, and eOptShrink successfully recovers the fetal ECG morphology even under arrhythmia, outperforming white-noise methods. The KV cache compression problem shares this structure: the residual ZZ carries meaningful per-token information with non-trivial covariance, making eOptShrink a natural fit. The key difference is that in fECG extraction, the goal is to recover ZZ (the fetal signal); here, we use the decomposition to improve quantization of ZZ by first removing the low-rank component SS.

From denoising to compression.

The connection to quantization becomes transparent through the lens of high-dimensional probability. When the entries of XX are i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d), each row xt∈ℝdx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfies the thin shell property (Vershynin, 2018): ‖xt‖2≈1\|x_{t}\|_{2}\approx 1 with high probability, and the normalized vector xt/‖xt‖x_{t}/\|x_{t}\| is approximately uniformly distributed on the unit sphere 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1}. Moreover, the coordinates are delocalized: the largest coordinate satisfies ‖xt‖∞≤C​log⁡d/d\|x_{t}\|_{\infty}\leq C\sqrt{\log d/d} with high probability for an absolute constant C>0C>0, meaning no single coordinate carries disproportionate energy (Vershynin, 2018, Problem 3.26). Multiplying by the deterministic matrices A1/2A^{1/2} and B1/2B^{1/2} rotates and stretches this sphere into an ellipsoid but preserves both the norm concentration and the delocalization—the rows of Z=A1/2​X​B1/2Z=A^{1/2}XB^{1/2} remain well-spread across coordinates with no outlier structure. These are precisely the conditions under which TQMSE’s random rotation plus Lloyd-Max quantization achieves near-optimal distortion: after normalizing each row and applying a Haar rotation, the coordinates become approximately i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d), matching the Lloyd-Max codebook.

The problem is the signal SS: its low-rank structure causes the rows of S~=S+Z\widetilde{S}=S+Z to cluster near a low-dimensional subspace, violating the isotropy that TQMSE requires. Our approach removes SS via optimal shrinkage, restoring the isotropic structure of ZZ. Let S^\hat{S} denote the eOptShrink estimate of SS (Algorithm 3). The residual R=S~−S^R=\widetilde{S}-\hat{S} approximates ZZ: its spectral distribution and Frobenius norm converge to those of ZZ (Proposition 6.1), and its rows inherit the thin shell and delocalization properties of ZZ (Corollary 6.3). Since ‖R‖F≈‖Z‖F<‖S~‖F\|R\|_{F}\approx\|Z\|_{F}<\|\widetilde{S}\|_{F} whenever SS has non-negligible energy, the inner product bias of TQMSE—which scales with the squared norm—is reduced by a factor of 1/(1+SNRt)1/(1+\mathrm{SNR}_{t}) compared to direct quantization (Proposition 6.1, Part 3), where SNRt:=∥S[t,:]∥2/∥Z[t,:]∥2\mathrm{SNR}_{t}:=\|S[t,:]\|^{2}/\|Z[t,:]\|^{2} is the per-token signal-to-noise ratio.

Contributions.

We make the following contributions:

On the theoretical side, we provide the first formalization of KV cache blocks as spiked random matrices: local context (h¯t\bar{h}_{t}) spans a low-dimensional subspace producing the low-rank signal SS, per-token variation (ϵt\epsilon_{t}) produces the residual ZZ with separable covariance, and both are projected through the deterministic WKW_{K}, preserving their independence. We show that the residual ZZ, whose rows arise from i.i.d. sub-Gaussian entries transformed by deterministic covariance matrices, satisfies the thin shell property: its rows have concentrated norms and delocalized coordinates, ‖rt‖∞≤C​log⁡d/d⋅‖rt‖2\|r_{t}\|_{\infty}\leq C\sqrt{\log d/d}\cdot\|r_{t}\|_{2} (Vershynin, 2018). The signal SS is the sole source of anisotropy that violates this property; removing it via optimal shrinkage restores the regime where per-vector scalar quantization is near-optimal, without requiring outlier handling or coordinate sub-grouping. We prove that this reduces inner product bias by a factor of 1/(1+SNRt)1/(1+\mathrm{SNR}_{t}) (Proposition 6.1), achieving near-zero bias so that all bb bits can be devoted to MSE reconstruction; QJL correction can optionally be added for further improvement. The rank and shrunken singular values are determined automatically by eOptShrink (Su and Wu, 2025) via the BBP phase transition, with no manual tuning and no knowledge of the noise covariance structure.

On the experimental side, we validate the spiked model predictions—outlier eigenvalues, bulk distribution, and phase transition—on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Ministral-8B-Instruct KV caches across all layers and heads. End-to-end on LongBench (16 tasks), eOptShrinkQMSE at ∼\sim2.2 bits achieves 47.4 (Llama) and 48.3 (Ministral), within 1.6 and 2.2 points of FP16 respectively—a 7×\times memory reduction with minimal quality loss. Even a simple rank-1 SVD at 2.04 bits matches standalone TQprod at 3.00 bits, demonstrating that spectral denoising is more effective than dedicating an extra bit to QJL correction.

2 Background

2.1 KV Cache in Transformer Attention

In multi-head attention, each layer computes queries QQ, keys KK, and values VV from the input hidden states. For an input sequence of length TT with head dimension dd:

Attention​(Q,K,V)=softmax​(Q​K⊤d)​V.\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V. (2)

During autoregressive generation, the KV cache stores all previously computed key and value vectors so they need not be recomputed. The cache grows linearly with sequence length, making compression essential for long-context inference.

2.2 TurboQuant

TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2025) compresses each dd-dimensional vector xx independently:

  1. 1.

    Norm separation: Store r=‖x‖r=\left\lVert x\right\rVert and work with u=x/ru=x/r on the unit sphere 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1}.

  2. 2.

    Random rotation: Apply a Haar-distributed random orthogonal matrix Π\Pi: z=Π​uz=\Pi u.

  3. 3.

    Scalar quantization: Quantize each coordinate of zz independently using a Lloyd-Max codebook (Lloyd, 1982; Max, 1960) optimized for the marginal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d) of rotated unit sphere coordinates.

  4. 4.

    Reconstruction: u^=Π⊤​z^\hat{u}=\Pi^{\top}\hat{z}, x^=r​u^\hat{x}=r\hat{u}.

The key insight is that after norm separation, the unit vector u=x/‖x‖u=x/\|x\| lies on 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1}. For uu uniformly distributed on 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1}, each coordinate of z=Π​uz=\Pi u follows a marginal distribution that converges to 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d) as d→∞d\to\infty (Zandieh et al., 2025, Lemma 1). The Lloyd-Max codebook, pre-computed for this Gaussian marginal, therefore achieves near-optimal scalar quantization distortion for each coordinate independently. The uniformity assumption on uu is critical: if the input vectors concentrate near a low-dimensional subspace rather than being uniformly spread on 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1}, the Gaussian approximation degrades and the codebook becomes suboptimal—a situation we address via spectral denoising.

We refer to this pipeline as TurboQuantMSE (denoted TQMSE, Algorithm 1): at bb bits per coordinate, it minimizes the mean squared reconstruction error 𝔼⁡[‖x−x^MSE‖2]\mathbb{E}[\|x-\hat{x}_{\text{MSE}}\|^{2}].

TQMSE minimizes mean squared reconstruction error 𝔼⁡[‖x−x^MSE‖2]\mathbb{E}[\|x-\hat{x}_{\text{MSE}}\|^{2}]. TQprod augments it with a 1-bit QJL correction for unbiased inner product estimation:

⟨y,x^⟩=⟨y,x^MSE⟩+‖rx‖⋅π/2d​⟨Φ​y,sign​(Φ​rx)⟩,\langle y,\hat{x}\rangle=\langle y,\hat{x}_{\text{MSE}}\rangle+\left\lVert r_{x}\right\rVert\cdot\frac{\sqrt{\pi/2}}{d}\langle\Phi y,\text{sign}(\Phi r_{x})\rangle, (3)

where rx=x−x^MSEr_{x}=x-\hat{x}_{\text{MSE}} is the quantization residual and Φ∈ℝd×d\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a random projection matrix with i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) entries. The first term ⟨y,x^MSE⟩\langle y,\hat{x}_{\text{MSE}}\rangle uses the MSE reconstruction, which is biased: the Lloyd-Max quantizer systematically shrinks each coordinate toward zero, so 𝔼⁡[⟨y,x^MSE⟩]<⟨y,x⟩\mathbb{E}[\langle y,\hat{x}_{\text{MSE}}\rangle]<\langle y,x\rangle. The second term corrects this bias by estimating the missing inner product ⟨y,rx⟩\langle y,r_{x}\rangle between the query and the quantization residual. The key insight is the Johnson–Lindenstrauss property: for a random projection Φ\Phi, the quantity 1d​⟨Φ​y,sign​(Φ​rx)⟩\frac{1}{d}\langle\Phi y,\text{sign}(\Phi r_{x})\rangle is an unbiased estimator of 2π​⟨y,rx/‖rx‖⟩\frac{2}{\pi}\langle y,r_{x}/\|r_{x}\|\rangle (Zandieh et al., 2025), requiring only 1 sign bit per coordinate to store sign​(Φ​rx)∈{−1,+1}d\text{sign}(\Phi r_{x})\in\{-1,+1\}^{d}. The scaling factor ‖rx‖⋅π/2/d\|r_{x}\|\cdot\sqrt{\pi/2}/d converts this to an unbiased estimate of ⟨y,rx⟩\langle y,r_{x}\rangle, yielding 𝔼⁡[⟨y,x^⟩]=⟨y,x⟩\mathbb{E}[\langle y,\hat{x}\rangle]=\langle y,x\rangle. The cost is one extra bit per coordinate and a 4×4\times increase in MSE distortion, since only bb of the b+1b+1 bits are used for reconstruction.

2.3 Optimal Singular Value Shrinkage

Given a data matrix S~=S+Z∈ℝn×d\widetilde{S}=S+Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} where S=∑i=1rdi​𝐮i​𝐯i⊤S=\sum_{i=1}^{r}d_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{\top} is a rank-rr signal with signal strengths d1≥⋯≥dr>0d_{1}\geq\cdots\geq d_{r}>0, left and right singular vectors 𝐮i∈ℝn\mathbf{u}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, 𝐯i∈ℝd\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and ZZ is a noise matrix, the goal is to recover SS from S~\widetilde{S}. Let S~=∑i=1n∧dσ~i​𝝃~i​𝜻~i⊤\widetilde{S}=\sum_{i=1}^{n\wedge d}\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}^{\top} be the SVD of the observed matrix, where λ~i:=σ~i2\tilde{\lambda}_{i}:=\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}^{2} are the eigenvalues of S~​S~⊤\widetilde{S}\widetilde{S}^{\top}. Singular value shrinkage (Donoho and Gavish, 2013; Donoho et al., 2018; Nadakuditi, 2014) constructs an estimate of SS by applying a nonlinear shrinker φ:[0,∞)→[0,∞)\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) to the observed singular values:

S^φ=∑i=1n∧dφ⁡(σ~i)​𝝃~i​𝜻~i⊤.\hat{S}_{\varphi}=\sum_{i=1}^{n\wedge d}\varphi(\widetilde{\sigma}_{i})\,\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}^{\top}. (4)

Given a loss function Ln:ℝn×d×ℝn×d→ℝ+L_{n}:\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} quantifying the discrepancy between S^φ\hat{S}_{\varphi} and SS (common choices include the Frobenius norm ‖S^φ−S‖F2/(n​d)\|\hat{S}_{\varphi}-S\|_{F}^{2}/(nd), operator norm, and nuclear norm), the optimal shrinker is defined as

φ∗:=arg​minφlimn→∞Ln(S^φ,S),\varphi^{*}:=\argmin_{\varphi}\lim_{n\to\infty}L_{n}(\hat{S}_{\varphi},S), (5)

where the limit is taken in the high-dimensional regime n/d→β∈(0,∞)n/d\to\beta\in(0,\infty) (Donoho et al., 2018).

In this regime, the observed singular values σ~i\widetilde{\sigma}_{i} are biased relative to the true signal strengths did_{i}: noise inflates the observed values, and weak signals become entangled with the noise bulk. The Marchenko–Pastur (MP) law (Marchenko and Pastur, 1967) describes the limiting spectral distribution of Z​Z⊤ZZ^{\top} when Z∈ℝn×dZ\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} has i.i.d. entries with mean zero, variance σ2/n\sigma^{2}/n, and finite fourth moment: the eigenvalues concentrate in a bulk supported on [λ−,λ+][\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+}], where λ±=σ2​(1±β)2\lambda_{\pm}=\sigma^{2}(1\pm\sqrt{\beta})^{2}. A phase transition (Baik et al., 2005) occurs at a critical signal strength α\alpha: signals with di>αd_{i}>\alpha produce outlier singular values that separate from the bulk and are detectable, while signals with di≤αd_{i}\leq\alpha are undetectable—their singular values “stick” to the bulk edge λ+\sqrt{\lambda_{+}}. The optimal shrinker depends on three quantities for each detectable signal (di>αd_{i}>\alpha): the signal strength did_{i} and the asymptotic singular vector overlaps

a1,i:=limn→∞|⟨𝐮i,𝝃~i⟩|2,a2,i:=limn→∞|⟨𝐯i,𝜻~i⟩|2,a_{1,i}:=\lim_{n\to\infty}|\langle\mathbf{u}_{i},\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\rangle|^{2},\qquad a_{2,i}:=\lim_{n\to\infty}|\langle\mathbf{v}_{i},\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}\rangle|^{2}, (6)

which quantify how well the noisy singular vectors 𝝃~i\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}, 𝜻~i\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i} approximate the true signal directions 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_{i}, 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i}. For the three standard loss functions (Donoho and Gavish, 2013; Leeb, 2022):

φi∗={di​a1,i​a2,i(Frobenius norm),di​a1,i∧a2,ia1,i∨a2,i(operator norm),di​(a1,i​a2,i−(1−a1,i)​(1−a2,i))(nuclear norm),\varphi^{*}_{i}=\begin{cases}d_{i}\sqrt{a_{1,i}a_{2,i}}&\text{(Frobenius norm)},\\[3.0pt] d_{i}\sqrt{\frac{a_{1,i}\wedge a_{2,i}}{a_{1,i}\vee a_{2,i}}}&\text{(operator norm)},\\[3.0pt] d_{i}\big(\sqrt{a_{1,i}a_{2,i}}-\sqrt{(1-a_{1,i})(1-a_{2,i})}\big)&\text{(nuclear norm)},\end{cases} (7)

and φi∗=0\varphi^{*}_{i}=0 when di≤αd_{i}\leq\alpha. Hard thresholding (truncated SVD) is a special case that retains the inflated σ~i\widetilde{\sigma}_{i} without correction—suboptimal because the retained values are biased upward by noise and the rank must be chosen manually.

Since the high-dimensional regime requires nn and dd to be comparable (n/d→βn/d\to\beta), we partition the KV cache into blocks of nn tokens with nn comparable to dd, and apply shrinkage independently to each block. This block-wise processing is natural for the streaming KV cache: as tokens arrive in chunks during prefill, each chunk forms a block that is compressed before the next chunk is processed.

When the noise has a separable covariance structure Z=A1/2​X​B1/2Z=A^{1/2}XB^{1/2} (as in KV cache blocks, where AA captures temporal dependence and BB captures coordinate covariance), the MP law no longer applies and the bulk edge λ+\lambda_{+} depends on both AA and BB. Standard optimal shrinkage methods (Donoho and Gavish, 2013; Donoho et al., 2018) assume white noise (A=B=IA=B=I) and fail in this setting. The eOptShrink estimator (Su and Wu, 2025) extends the OptShrink framework (Nadakuditi, 2014) to handle colored noise with separable covariance, non-square matrices, and automatic rank determination—all essential for KV cache blocks where n≠dn\neq d and the residual statistics are non-white. The algorithm (Algorithm 2) is fully data-driven. It estimates the bulk edge λ^+\hat{\lambda}_{+} and effective rank r^+\hat{r}^{+} from the observed spectrum, recovers the noise spectral distribution F^e\hat{F}_{e} by imputing the eigenvalues perturbed by signals, and computes the data-driven estimates of did_{i}, a1,ia_{1,i}, a2,ia_{2,i}. Central to the algorithm is the DD-transform (Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi, 2012):

𝒯⁡(z):=z​m1​c​(z)​m2​c​(z),\mathcal{T}(z):=z\,m_{1c}(z)\,m_{2c}(z), (8)

where m1​c​(z)m_{1c}(z) and m2​c​(z)m_{2c}(z) are the Stieltjes transforms of the asymptotic limiting spectral measures of Z​Z⊤ZZ^{\top} and Z⊤​ZZ^{\top}Z respectively. The Stieltjes transform of a measure μ\mu is mμ​(z):=∫(x−z)−1​𝑑μ​(x)m_{\mu}(z):=\int(x-z)^{-1}d\mu(x) for z∈ℂ+z\in\mathbb{C}^{+}; see (Su and Wu, 2025, Section 2) for the precise definitions of m1​cm_{1c}, m2​cm_{2c} in terms of the noise covariance matrices AA and BB. Since neither AA, BB, nor the noise spectral distribution are known, eOptShrink estimates them from the data. The estimated noise spectral distribution F^e\hat{F}_{e} is the empirical CDF of the estimated noise eigenvalues:

F^e(x)=1n∧d∑i=1n∧d𝟏{λ^e,i≤x},\hat{F}_{e}(x)=\frac{1}{n\wedge d}\sum_{i=1}^{n\wedge d}\mathbf{1}\{\hat{\lambda}_{e,i}\leq x\}, (9)

where λ^e,i=λ~i\hat{\lambda}_{e,i}=\tilde{\lambda}_{i} for i>r^++ki>\hat{r}^{+}+k (non-outlier, non-perturbed eigenvalues used directly), and the top r^++k\hat{r}^{+}+k eigenvalues are replaced by imputed values: the r^+\hat{r}^{+} outlier eigenvalues are discarded, and the next kk eigenvalues (perturbed by proximity to the outliers) are imputed using the square-root edge behavior of the bulk (Step 2 of Algorithm 2). The estimated Stieltjes transforms m^e,1,i\hat{m}_{e,1,i}, m^e,2,i\hat{m}_{e,2,i} and DD-transform 𝒯^e,i:=λ~i​m^e,1,i​m^e,2,i\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{e,i}:=\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\,\hat{m}_{e,1,i}\,\hat{m}_{e,2,i} are then evaluated from F^e\hat{F}_{e}. For each 1≤i≤r^+1\leq i\leq\hat{r}^{+}, the estimators are (Su and Wu, 2025):

d^e,i=1𝒯^e,i,a^e,1,i=m^e,1,id^e,i2​𝒯^e,i′,a^e,2,i=m^e,2,id^e,i2​𝒯^e,i′,\hat{d}_{e,i}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{e,i}}},\quad\hat{a}_{e,1,i}=\frac{\hat{m}_{e,1,i}}{\hat{d}_{e,i}^{2}\,\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\prime}_{e,i}},\quad\hat{a}_{e,2,i}=\frac{\hat{m}_{e,2,i}}{\hat{d}_{e,i}^{2}\,\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\prime}_{e,i}}, (10)

where 𝒯^e,i′\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\prime}_{e,i} is the derivative of 𝒯^e\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{e} at λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i}. These are plugged into (7) to obtain the shrunken values φ^e,i\hat{\varphi}_{e,i}, yielding S^=∑i=1r^+φ^e,i​𝝃~i​𝜻~i⊤\hat{S}=\sum_{i=1}^{\hat{r}^{+}}\hat{\varphi}_{e,i}\,\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}^{\top}. Crucially, the algorithm requires no knowledge of AA, BB, or the rank rr—all are estimated from the data.

3 Method

The eOptShrinkQ pipeline processes the KV cache in blocks of nn tokens (Algorithm 3). Each block S~∈ℝn×d\widetilde{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} is first denoised via eOptShrink (Algorithm 2), which automatically determines the rank r^+\hat{r}^{+} and computes the Frobenius-norm-optimal shrunken singular values. If no eigenvalue exceeds the bulk edge (r^+=0\hat{r}^{+}=0), the block is passed directly to TQMSE without SVD preprocessing. Otherwise, the low-rank estimate S^\hat{S} is subtracted, and the residual R=S~−S^R=\widetilde{S}-\hat{S} is quantized row-by-row via TQMSE (Algorithm 1). Optionally, QJL correction can be added for keys (upgrading to TQprod), and SVD factors can be quantized at bsb_{s} bits to reduce overhead.

Remark 3.1 (Automatic rank selection).

Rather than using a fixed rank, eOptShrink determines the rank and shrunken singular values automatically from the data via the BBP phase transition threshold, without requiring knowledge of the noise covariance. When no eigenvalue exceeds the bulk edge (r^+=0\hat{r}^{+}=0), the block is entirely isotropic and passed directly to TQMSE—avoiding unnecessary SVD overhead on blocks without detectable low-rank structure. In all experiments, we use the Frobenius norm loss and set c=min⁡(1/2.01, 1/log⁡(log⁡d))c=\min(1/2.01,\,1/\log(\log d)); for d=128d=128 this gives pilot parameter k=11k=11. SVD factors are quantized at 4 bits via data-adaptive Lloyd-Max codebooks. The bit budget formula in Algorithm 3 accounts for the residual quantization (bb bits per entry) and the SVD factor overhead (r^+​(n+d)​bs/(n​d)\hat{r}^{+}(n{+}d)b_{s}/(nd)). Two additional small costs are shared across all TQ-based methods and cancel in comparisons: (1) TQ stores one FP16 norm per row (16/d16/d bits per entry, i.e., 0.1250.125 for d=128d=128), and (2) the shrunken singular values Σ^\hat{\Sigma} are stored at FP16 (16​r^+/(n​d)16\hat{r}^{+}/(nd) bits per entry, negligible since r^+≪min⁡(n,d)\hat{r}^{+}\ll\min(n,d)).

4 Numerical Experiments

We conduct numerical experiments on two model families to validate the compression pipeline: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) (d=128d=128, 32 layers ×\times 8 KV heads) and Ministral-8B-Instruct (Liu et al., 2026) (d=128d=128, 36 layers ×\times 8 KV heads). We first evaluate per-head reconstruction quality (Section 4.1), then end-to-end performance on LongBench and multi-needle retrieval (Section 4.2).

Methods compared.

We compare the following approaches:

  • •

    KIVI (Liu et al., 2024): per-channel asymmetric quantization for keys (axis=0) and per-token for values (axis=1), with group size 64. This is the most widely adopted KV cache quantization baseline. Total bits include the group-wise scale and zero-point overhead (32/g32/g bits per entry for group size gg).

  • •

    TQMSE: standalone TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2025) with MSE-optimal Lloyd-Max quantization (Section 2.2).

  • •

    TQprod: TurboQuant with bb-bit MSE plus 1-bit QJL correction for unbiased inner products (b+1b+1 total bits).

  • •

    SVDr=1 + TQMSE: rank-1 truncated SVD to remove the leading singular component, then TQMSE on the residual. This baseline isolates the effect of removing even a single dominant direction, at negligible bit overhead (0.04 bits), and demonstrates the value of spectral denoising in its simplest form.

  • •

    eOptShrinkQMSE: optimal shrinkage with data-adaptive rank (Section 3.1), then TQMSE on the residual. Optionally, eOptShrinkQprod replaces TQMSE with TQprod on the residual for additional QJL correction.

SVD factors are quantized at 4 bits in all experiments. All blocks use sequential (causal) token ordering.

No sub-grouping or outlier handling.

Unlike the original TurboQuant implementation (Zandieh et al., 2025) and other quantization approaches that partition coordinates into sub-vectors of different sizes and handle outlier channels separately, we apply TQMSE to the full dd-dimensional vector without sub-grouping. After eOptShrink removes the low-rank signal, the residual rows satisfy the delocalization bound ‖rt‖∞≤C​log⁡d/d⋅‖rt‖2\|r_{t}\|_{\infty}\leq C\sqrt{\log d/d}\cdot\|r_{t}\|_{2} (Corollary 6.3): no coordinate is an outlier, so sub-grouping is unnecessary. For fair comparison, all methods—including the TQMSE and TQprod baselines—use the same full-vector quantization without sub-grouping.

4.1 KV Cache Compression Quality

We run Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Ministral-8B-Instruct (Liu et al., 2026) on a LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) QAsper passage (∼\sim3000 tokens) and extract the full KV cache after prefill. We evaluate compression across all layers and KV heads (Llama: 32 layers ×\times 8 heads == 256 heads; Ministral: 36 layers ×\times 8 heads == 288 heads), with d=128d=128 and blocks of 128×128128\times 128.

Spiked model validation and spectral denoising.

We verify that the spiked model S~=S+Z\widetilde{S}=S+Z accurately describes the spectral structure of KV cache blocks, and visualize the effect of eOptShrink. In the spiked model, the effective rank r+r^{+} is the number of signal singular values strong enough to separate from the noise bulk (i.e., exceeding the BBP phase transition threshold α\alpha; see Appendix A.2). eOptShrink estimates this as r^+\widehat{r}^{+}—the number of singular values exceeding the estimated bulk edge λ^+\sqrt{\widehat{\lambda}_{+}}—without requiring knowledge of the noise distribution (Algorithm 2). Figures 1 and 3 show representative key heads on Llama (L15H3) and Ministral (L5H3): the top row displays the singular value spectrum and distribution, while the bottom row shows heatmaps of the original block S~\widetilde{S}, the extracted signal S^\hat{S}, and the residual R=S~−S^R=\widetilde{S}-\hat{S}. In both models, outlier singular values clearly separate above the bulk edge, and the heatmaps reveal prominent vertical stripes in S~\widetilde{S}—per-channel outliers that KIVI’s per-channel quantization is designed to handle. The rank-r^+\hat{r}^{+} signal S^\hat{S} captures precisely these stripes, and the residual RR is visually isotropic with no discernible structure. This confirms that eOptShrink removes the anisotropy at its source rather than engineering around its symptoms.

Figures 2 and 4 show the corresponding analysis for value heads (Llama L31H0, Ministral L18H1). The spiked structure is also present, with outlier singular values separating from the bulk. The heatmaps show visible column and row patterns in S~\widetilde{S}, captured by S^\hat{S} and absent from RR. The bulk edge estimator λ^+\sqrt{\widehat{\lambda}_{+}} correctly delineates the boundary for both keys and values on both models, confirming that eOptShrink’s automatic rank estimation generalizes across model families.

We report relative L2L_{2} error ‖X^−X‖F/‖X‖F\|\hat{X}-X\|_{F}/\|X\|_{F} (in percent), inner product (IP) bias, and IP standard deviation on unit-normalized vectors (cosine similarity error). These per-head metrics isolate quantization fidelity from confounding factors in downstream evaluation (prompt formatting, generation strategy, task-specific scoring) and enable direct comparison across methods with different quantization strategies. Tables 1 and 2 show the results for Llama; Tables 3 and 4 for Ministral.

Tables 1–4 demonstrate four findings consistent across both models and both keys and values.

eOptShrinkQ outperforms KIVI at fewer bits. KIVI (Liu et al., 2024) uses per-channel quantization for keys and per-token quantization for values, with group-wise scales adding 0.50.5 bits overhead (group size 64). On keys, eOptShrinkQMSE at 2.35 bits achieves 17.7% L2L_{2} versus KIVI’s 24.8% at 2.50 bits—a 29% relative reduction with fewer bits. On values, KIVI’s per-token quantization is particularly ineffective at low bit rates: 49.5% L2L_{2} at 2.50 bits versus TQMSE’s 34.1% at 2.00 bits, because per-token quantization does not exploit the random rotation that TurboQuant uses to isotropize each vector before scalar quantization. KIVI’s asymmetric treatment of keys versus values (different quantization axes) is an engineering response to the anisotropy caused by the low-rank structure; our approach removes the root cause, enabling uniform treatment with a single quantizer. We note that KIVI’s advantage lies in hardware efficiency: its per-channel INT quantization maps directly to tensor core operations, whereas TurboQuant’s Lloyd-Max codebooks require lookup tables. Our contribution is orthogonal—spectral denoising can in principle be combined with any downstream quantizer, including hardware-friendly INT schemes.

eOptShrinkQ saves nearly one bit per entry over TurboQuant. At every bit rate, eOptShrinkQMSE achieves the lowest L2L_{2} error and IP standard deviation. Notably, eOptShrinkQMSE at b=2b=2 (2.35 total bits) achieves 17.7% L2L_{2} on Llama keys—substantially better than KIVI at 2.50 bits (24.8%) and TQMSE at 2.00 bits (34.1%). At b=3b=3, eOptShrinkQMSE at 3.35 bits (9.6% L2L_{2}) outperforms TQMSE at 4.00 bits (9.7%)—achieving better reconstruction with 0.65 fewer bits. This bit saving comes from the spectral denoising: by extracting the low-rank structure (r¯≈5\bar{r}\approx 5–66), the residual becomes more isotropic and TQMSE operates closer to its theoretical optimum. The SVD overhead is r^+​(n+d)​bs/(n​d)\hat{r}^{+}(n{+}d)b_{s}/(nd) bits per entry (Algorithm 3): for SVDr=1 with n=128n=128, d=128d=128, bs=4b_{s}=4, this is 1×256×4/16384≈0.061\times 256\times 4/16384\approx 0.06 bits; for eOptShrinkQ with r¯≈5.6\bar{r}\approx 5.6, approximately 0.350.35 bits.

QJL correction is largely unnecessary after spectral denoising. TQprod eliminates IP bias but at a cost: it increases IP standard deviation compared to TQMSE at the same MSE bit rate (e.g., .036.036 vs. .026.026 at b=2b=2 on Llama keys), because the QJL correction trades bias for variance. eOptShrinkQMSE achieves near-zero bias (+.006+.006 at b=2b=2, vanishing at b=4b=4) and the lowest IP standard deviation simultaneously—without spending any bits on QJL. Adding QJL on top (eOptShrinkQprod) drives the bias to exactly zero but increases the variance, making it a marginal improvement at best.

Automatic rank selection is essential. SVDr=1 truncation already provides a large improvement over TQMSE (e.g., 21.2% vs. 34.1% L2L_{2} at b=2b=2 on Llama keys), demonstrating the value of removing even a single dominant component. However, eOptShrinkQ with adaptive rank r¯≈5\bar{r}\approx 5–66 reduces the error further to 17.8%—a 16% relative improvement over SVDr=1. The gap is even larger on values, where the spectral structure is distributed across more components: on Llama values at b=2b=2, eOptShrinkQ achieves 26.4% vs. SVDr=1’s 30.4%. The higher rank extracts more shared structure, leaving a more isotropic residual that TQMSE compresses more efficiently.

4.2 End-to-End Evaluation

We evaluate end-to-end on LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) (16 English tasks) and multi-needle retrieval using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Ministral-8B-Instruct (Liu et al., 2026). Compression is applied chunk-by-chunk during prefill: each chunk of 128 tokens passes through all layers in FP16, then the KV cache for that chunk is compressed in-place using blocks of 128×128128\times 128. Both keys and values are compressed at the same bit rate bb. This captures two levels of error accumulation: between layers, where layer l+1l+1 computes its hidden states from layer ll’s compressed attention output, and between chunks, where subsequent chunks attend over already-compressed cache from all previous chunks. For a sequence of TT tokens with LL layers, compression errors propagate through ⌊T/128⌋×L\lfloor T/128\rfloor\times L compression-then-attend steps.

LongBench. Table 5 shows category-averaged scores across all 16 tasks. eOptShrinkQMSE at ∼\sim2.2 bits achieves 47.4 on Llama and 48.3 on Ministral—within 1.6 and 2.2 points of FP16 respectively, and outperforming TQprod at 3.0 bits (45.2 and 46.6) despite using substantially fewer bits. eOptShrinkQMSE wins 4 of 6 categories on both models, with especially large gains on MultiQA (+4.8+4.8 over TQMSE on Llama) and Code (+4.7+4.7), where precise retrieval of specific tokens across long contexts is essential. On Code, eOptShrinkQMSE at 2.2 bits (53.9) matches FP16 (53.1), suggesting that spectral regularization can benefit retrieval-intensive tasks. Adding QJL (eOptShrinkQprod at ∼\sim3.2 bits) provides a small further gain to 47.6, primarily on Summarization and SingleQA.

Multi-Needle Retrieval. Needle-in-a-Haystack (Schuster et al., 2025) tests whether a model can retrieve a planted fact from a long context. We extend this to the multi-needle setting: NN distinct facts are scattered at evenly spaced positions throughout the context, and the model must retrieve all NN simultaneously. Figures 5 and 6 show recall heatmaps across N=2,4,6,8,10N=2,4,6,8,10 needles and context lengths from 4K to 104K tokens (Llama) and 4K to 30K (Ministral). eOptShrinkQMSE at 2.2 bits achieves 0.981 average recall on Llama—outperforming FP16 (0.972)—and 0.992 on Ministral, nearly matching FP16 (1.000). The heatmaps reveal that SVDr=1 produces scattered failures across lengths and needle counts (average 0.886 on Llama), while eOptShrinkQMSE maintains near-perfect recall throughout. TQprod at 3.0 bits is the worst method on both models (0.940 and 0.938), as the QJL correction increases inner product variance that accumulates across the many compressed tokens the model must attend over during multi-fact retrieval.

5 Analysis

We highlight three observations from the experiments that connect to the theoretical framework.

Spectral regularization. On tasks requiring precise token-level retrieval, eOptShrinkQMSE matches or exceeds FP16: Code on Llama (53.9 vs. 53.1) and multi-needle retrieval on Llama (0.981 vs. 0.972). This effect is task-dependent: on Summarization, which requires integrating shared context across the entire passage, eOptShrinkQMSE slightly underperforms FP16 (27.4 vs. 29.2 on Llama). The pattern suggests that removing the low-rank shared context acts as a form of spectral regularization: it reduces the effective dimension of the attention computation, benefiting tasks where attention must discriminate among many similar token representations (retrieval, code) while slightly degrading tasks that rely on global context integration (summarization). Notably, eOptShrinkQprod at 3.22 bits partially recovers the summarization gap (28.5 vs. 29.2), suggesting that the QJL correction specifically helps tasks where preserving the shared structure’s contribution to inner products matters. On Ministral, eOptShrinkQMSE closely tracks FP16 across all categories without exceeding it, suggesting the regularization effect is model- and task-dependent rather than a universal property.

QJL correction trades bias for variance. TQprod achieves near-zero IP bias but at the cost of increased IP standard deviation (e.g., .036.036 vs. .026.026 for TQMSE at b=2b=2 on Llama keys, Table 1). On downstream tasks, this trade-off is unfavorable: TQprod is consistently the worst method on multi-needle retrieval (0.940 on Llama, 0.938 on Ministral), because the variance from QJL correction accumulates across the many compressed tokens that the model must attend over during generation. eOptShrinkQMSE achieves near-zero bias and the lowest variance simultaneously, without spending any bits on QJL. This explains why eOptShrinkQMSE at 2.22 bits outperforms TQprod at 3.0 bits across all evaluations.

Adaptive rank across layers. The effective rank r^+\hat{r}^{+} selected by eOptShrink varies across layers and heads: on Llama keys (n=128n=128, d=128d=128), we observe r^+≈9\hat{r}^{+}\approx 9 in early layers, r^+≈11\hat{r}^{+}\approx 11 in middle layers, and r^+≈5\hat{r}^{+}\approx 5 in the final layer. This variation reflects the changing nature of contextual structure across the network: middle layers tend to carry richer semantic representations, while final layers are more diffuse—a pattern consistent with the spectral analysis of KV caches reported in CSKV (Wang et al., 2024). Fixed-rank methods like SVDr=1 cannot capture this variation, which explains their inferior performance especially on values (r¯≈5\bar{r}\approx 5) where the low-rank structure is distributed across more components than a single direction.

6 Theoretical Guarantees

We now formalize the key theoretical result: after optimal shrinkage, the residual enters the regime where per-vector scalar quantization achieves near-optimal distortion with negligible inner product bias. We state the result under the spiked model S~=S+Z\widetilde{S}=S+Z with separable noise covariance Z=A1/2​X​B1/2Z=A^{1/2}XB^{1/2} (Eq. (14)–(15)), assuming signal strengths exceed the BBP phase transition threshold and signal directions are independent of the noise. The precise technical conditions (moment bounds, aspect ratio, covariance regularity) are given in Assumption A.1 in Appendix A.2. We use the stochastic dominance notation ξ≺ζ\xi\prec\zeta to denote high-probability bounds up to sub-polynomial factors (Appendix A.3).

Proposition 6.1 (Residual isotropy after optimal shrinkage).

Under Assumption A.1 (which treats signal singular vectors as random; see Remark A.3 for the scope of this assumption at inference time), let S^\hat{S} be the eOptShrink estimate of SS from (14), and let R=S~−S^R=\widetilde{S}-\hat{S} be the residual. Denote the rows of S~\widetilde{S}, S^\hat{S}, RR, and ZZ as xtx_{t}, s^t\hat{s}_{t}, rtr_{t}, and ztz_{t} respectively for t=1,…,nt=1,\ldots,n. Then:

  1. 1.

    (Residual spectrum matches noise.) The empirical spectral distribution of R​R⊤RR^{\top} converges to that of Z​Z⊤ZZ^{\top}; in particular, RR has no outlier singular values.

  2. 2.

    (Reduced Frobenius norm.) The residual energy concentrates at the noise level:

    |1n​d‖R‖F2−1n​d‖Z‖F2|≺ϕd+d−1/2/Δmin,\left|\frac{1}{nd}\left\lVert R\right\rVert_{F}^{2}-\frac{1}{nd}\left\lVert Z\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\right|\prec\phi_{d}+d^{-1/2}/\Delta_{\min}, (11)

    where Δmin:=min1≤i≤r+⁡Δ⁡(di)\Delta_{\min}:=\min_{1\leq i\leq r^{+}}\Delta(d_{i}). In particular, ‖R‖F2=‖Z‖F2+O≺(nd⋅(ϕd+d−1/2/Δmin))\left\lVert R\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\left\lVert Z\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+O_{\prec}(nd\cdot(\phi_{d}+d^{-1/2}/\Delta_{\min})), so ‖R‖F<‖S~‖F\left\lVert R\right\rVert_{F}<\left\lVert\widetilde{S}\right\rVert_{F} whenever the signal has non-negligible energy.

  3. 3.

    (Inner product bias reduction.) Let q∈ℝdq\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be a query vector, and let r~t\tilde{r}_{t} be the TurboQuantMSE reconstruction of rtr_{t} at bb bits. The inner product bias of the shrinkage-based pipeline is reduced by a factor of 1/(1+SNRt)1/(1+\mathrm{SNR}_{t}) compared to direct quantization:

    |𝔼⁡[⟨q,r~t⟩]−⟨q,rt⟩||𝔼⁡[⟨q,x~t⟩]−⟨q,xt⟩|≤‖rt‖2‖xt‖2≤11+SNRt+o≺​(1),\frac{|\mathbb{E}[\langle q,\tilde{r}_{t}\rangle]-\langle q,r_{t}\rangle|}{|\mathbb{E}[\langle q,\tilde{x}_{t}\rangle]-\langle q,x_{t}\rangle|}\leq\frac{\left\lVert r_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}{\left\lVert x_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{1+\mathrm{SNR}_{t}}+o_{\prec}(1), (12)

    where SNRt:=‖st‖2/‖zt‖2\mathrm{SNR}_{t}:=\left\lVert s_{t}\right\rVert^{2}/\left\lVert z_{t}\right\rVert^{2} is the per-token signal-to-noise ratio.

Part 1 follows from the eigenvalue sticking theorem and delocalization of non-outlier singular vectors (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorems 3.3–3.4); Part 2 from concentration of the cross term ⟨S−S^,Z⟩F\langle S-\hat{S},Z\rangle_{F}; Part 3 from applying TurboQuant’s bias bound (Theorem 1 of Zandieh et al. (2025)) to the residual versus the original vector. The full proof is given in Appendix A.6.

Remark 6.2 (Why QJL becomes unnecessary).

The delocalization property is the theoretical reason why QJL correction becomes unnecessary after shrinkage. TurboQuantprod’s QJL correction guarantees unbiased IP estimation for any input, but costs 1 bit per coordinate. After eOptShrink, the residual rows rtr_{t} have small norms and delocalized spectral structure—precisely the regime where TurboQuantMSE’s bias is already negligible. Spending that bit on MSE quality (which scales as 4−b4^{-b}) yields a 4×4\times improvement in distortion compared to dedicating it to QJL.

Corollary 6.3 (Coordinate delocalization of residual rows).

Under Assumption A.1, the rows of the residual R=S~−S^R=\widetilde{S}-\hat{S} satisfy the following coordinate delocalization: for each row t=1,…,nt=1,\ldots,n,

‖rt‖∞‖rt‖2≤C​log⁡dd\frac{\|r_{t}\|_{\infty}}{\|r_{t}\|_{2}}\leq C\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{d}} (13)

with high probability, where C>0C>0 is an absolute constant. In particular, the unit-normed residual rows rt/‖rt‖r_{t}/\|r_{t}\| are approximately uniformly distributed on the sphere 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1} in the sense that no coordinate carries disproportionate energy, which is the precondition for TurboQuant’s near-optimal quantization (Zandieh et al., 2025, Lemma 1).

The proof is given in Appendix A.7.

Remark 6.4 (Why shrinkage improves quantization).

TQMSE assumes each input vector is approximately uniform on 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1} (Zandieh et al., 2025, Lemma 1). KV cache vectors violate this: within a block, unit-normed directions cluster around the dominant right singular vectors of S~\widetilde{S}, so after random rotation the coordinate marginals are no longer i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d) and the Lloyd-Max codebook becomes suboptimal. By removing SS via eOptShrink, the residual rows satisfy the thin shell and delocalization properties of ZZ (Section 1, Corollary 6.3), restoring the uniformity assumption. The low-rank component SS is stored separately via quantized SVD factors at negligible overhead.

Remark 6.5 (Inner product bias reduction).

The MSE quantizer produces a negative IP bias 𝔼⁡[⟨y,x~⟩]<⟨y,x⟩\mathbb{E}[\langle y,\tilde{x}\rangle]<\langle y,x\rangle that scales with ‖x‖2\left\lVert x\right\rVert^{2}. Our decomposition ⟨y,x⟩=⟨y,x^⟩+⟨y,r⟩\langle y,x\rangle=\langle y,\hat{x}\rangle+\langle y,r\rangle splits this into: (1) the low-rank term ⟨y,x^⟩\langle y,\hat{x}\rangle, computed from precisely stored SVD factors with negligible error, and (2) the residual term ⟨y,r⟩\langle y,r\rangle, quantized via TQMSE with bias scaling as ‖r‖2≪‖x‖2\left\lVert r\right\rVert^{2}\ll\left\lVert x\right\rVert^{2}. Since the bias is reduced by a factor of 1/(1+SNRt)1/(1+\mathrm{SNR}_{t}) (Proposition 6.1, Part 3), all bb bits can be devoted to MSE reconstruction. QJL correction (TQprod) can optionally be added on top for further improvement.

7 Related Work

KV Cache Quantization.

Several approaches have been proposed to reduce KV cache memory through quantization. KIVI (Liu et al., 2024) uses per-channel quantization with 2-bit keys and 5-bit values. KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024) extends this with per-channel rotation and non-uniform datatypes. PolarQuant (Han et al., 2025) applies polar transformation before quantization. GEAR (Kang et al., 2024) quantizes the bulk of KV entries to ultra-low precision, then approximates the quantization error with a low-rank matrix and corrects outliers with a sparse matrix—an error-correction approach that is complementary to our signal-extraction pipeline. Dynamic Memory Compression (Nawrot et al., 2024) merges KV cache entries via learned aggregation. SnapKV (Li et al., 2024b) and PyramidKV (Cai et al., 2024) use attention-based token eviction to reduce cache size. Our approach is complementary to eviction and merging methods: quantization reduces per-token cost while eviction and merging reduce token count.

Low-Rank KV Cache Compression.

A growing body of work applies SVD to KV caches for dimensionality reduction: Palu (Chang et al., 2024) decomposes KV projection weights via SVD to cache lower-dimensional intermediate states; CSKV (Wang et al., 2024) analyzes the singular value distribution of KV caches and applies low-rank decomposition to shrink channels; SVDq (Yankun et al., 2025) projects keys into an SVD basis with importance-aware quantization of latent channels; xKV (Chang et al., 2025) exploits cross-layer singular vector alignment for shared-basis compression; and OjaKV (Zhu et al., 2025) uses online PCA via Oja’s rule for adaptive low-rank projection.

Our approach differs fundamentally from the above. These methods use SVD for dimensionality reduction: they project KV vectors into a lower-dimensional subspace, store the compressed representation, and reconstruct at inference time. In contrast, we use SVD for spectral denoising before quantization: the residual after optimal shrinkage remains full-dimensional and is quantized by a downstream per-vector scalar quantizer. The low-rank component is a preprocessing step that restores the isotropy assumptions required by the quantizer, rather than the compression mechanism itself. Furthermore, all existing methods use truncated SVD with fixed or heuristically chosen rank and unmodified singular values, whereas eOptShrink provides theoretically optimal rank selection via the BBP phase transition and noise-aware singular value shrinkage—a qualitatively different treatment grounded in random matrix theory.

Vector Quantization.

Product quantization (PQ) (Han et al., 2025) partitions coordinates into sub-vectors and quantizes each independently. RaBitQ (Gao and Long, 2024) uses random rotation plus 1-bit quantization with bias correction, similar in spirit to TurboQuant. The idea of applying random rotations (e.g., Hadamard transforms) to achieve incoherence before quantization also appears in weight quantization methods such as QuIP (Tseng et al., 2024); our spectral denoising achieves a similar isotropy-restoring effect through a different mechanism—removing the low-rank structure rather than rotating it. Our approach can be combined with any downstream scalar quantizer.

Low-Rank Approximation + Quantization.

SVDQuant (Li et al., 2024a) pioneered the idea of combining SVD with quantization for neural network compression: they apply truncated SVD to weight matrices to separate outlier directions into a full-precision low-rank branch, then quantize the residual to 4 bits. However, SVDQuant uses a fixed rank chosen by grid search and does not modify the singular values. Our work differs in three key ways: (1) we target KV caches rather than weights, (2) we use eOptShrink (Su and Wu, 2025) for automatic, data-adaptive rank selection and optimal singular value shrinkage, and (3) we pair the residual with TurboQuant’s near-optimal scalar quantizer rather than per-group INT4. The automatic rank selection is particularly important for KV caches, where the effective rank varies across layers, heads, and input sequences. Other SVD-based weight compression methods (Hsu et al., 2022) share the fixed-rank limitation. The streaming nature of KV caches (tokens arrive sequentially) requires block-wise processing, which our approach handles naturally.

Optimal Shrinkage.

The theory of optimal singular value shrinkage originates from random matrix theory (Marchenko and Pastur, 1967). Gavish and Donoho (Donoho and Gavish, 2013) derived optimal hard thresholds. Donoho, Gavish, and Johnstone (Donoho et al., 2018) established the optimal shrinkage of eigenvalues in the spiked covariance model, providing the theoretical foundation for data-driven singular value shrinkage under high-dimensional noise. Nadakuditi (Nadakuditi, 2014) developed OptShrink, extending optimal shrinkage to general noise distributions. In our prior work (Su and Wu, 2025), we further extended the framework to non-square matrices and colored noise with separable covariance structure (eOptShrink), with automatic rank estimation. Here we apply these tools to KV cache compression for the first time.

8 Conclusion

We have presented eOptShrinkQ, a KV cache compression method grounded in the spiked random matrix framework. The key insight is that KV cache blocks decompose into a low-rank shared context component and a full-rank per-token residual satisfying the thin shell property. The shared context is the sole source of anisotropy that degrades per-vector scalar quantization; removing it via optimal shrinkage restores the isotropy under which the quantizer operates at its theoretical optimum, without requiring outlier handling or sub-grouping. The approach is complementary to any downstream per-vector quantizer—we demonstrate it with TurboQuant and expect similar benefits with other quantizers.

eOptShrinkQ saves nearly one bit per entry over TurboQuant at equivalent reconstruction quality, achieving per-head L2L_{2} error at 3.22 bits that surpasses TurboQuant at 4.00 bits. End-to-end on LongBench, eOptShrinkQ at ∼\sim2.2 bits outperforms TurboQuant at 3.0 bits on both Llama-3.1-8B and Ministral-8B. On retrieval-intensive tasks (multi-needle, code completion), eOptShrinkQ at 2.2 bits closely matches or exceeds FP16 quality, suggesting that spectral denoising acts as a beneficial regularizer by removing redundant shared structure that can interfere with fine-grained token discrimination. This effect is task-dependent: tasks requiring global context integration (summarization) show slightly reduced performance, consistent with removing genuinely useful shared structure.

Computational overhead.

The spectral denoising adds O⁡(n​d​min⁡(n,d))O(nd\min(n,d)) per block during prefill, which is of the same or lower order as the per-vector TurboQuant compression (O⁡(n​d2)O(nd^{2}) per block), and both are negligible compared to the attention computation O⁡(T2​d)O(T^{2}d) at long context lengths. Importantly, the compression cost is incurred only during prefill; at inference time, the compressed KV cache is a standard dense tensor with no additional per-token overhead (unlike QJL correction, which requires extra computation during generation).

Limitations and Future Work.

Our current evaluation uses block-wise processing with blocks of n=128n=128 tokens, which requires buffering tokens before compression. During prefill (processing a long prompt), 128-token chunks arise naturally and eOptShrinkQ compresses each chunk as it completes. During autoregressive generation, tokens arrive one at a time; newly generated tokens are accumulated in an FP16 buffer until a full 128-token block is formed, at which point the block is compressed. This means the most recent ≤127\leq 127 tokens are always stored in FP16—a minor overhead at long contexts (e.g., <0.13%<0.13\% of cache at 100K tokens) but a real limitation for short generation sequences. Online SVD updates that incrementally maintain the rank estimate and shrunken factors as tokens arrive would eliminate this buffering requirement, but adapting the BBP phase transition test and noise spectral estimation to the streaming setting remains an open problem. Extending to larger models (70B+), integrating with other KV cache reduction techniques (token eviction, cross-layer sharing), and developing hardware-aware implementations with latency benchmarks are natural next steps.

Implementation details.

All experiments are conducted on a server with 8×\times NVIDIA A6000 GPUs (48GB each), CUDA 12.0, PyTorch 2.1.2. Models are loaded in FP16. eOptShrinkQ is implemented in PyTorch. Code will be made publicly available.

Appendix A Technical Details

This appendix provides the precise technical conditions underlying Proposition 6.1, the supporting theorems from random matrix theory, the eOptShrink algorithm, and the full proof.

A.1 Spiked Model for KV Cache Blocks

Consider a block of nn row vectors (keys, values, or embeddings) from a single attention head, forming a data matrix S~∈ℝn×d\widetilde{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}. We model S~\widetilde{S} as a low-rank signal plus residual:

S~=S+Z=∑i=1rdi​𝐮i​𝐯i⊤+Z∈ℝn×d,\widetilde{S}=S+Z=\sum_{i=1}^{r}d_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{\top}+Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, (14)

where SS is the low-rank signal capturing shared structure across rows, rr is the signal rank, di>0d_{i}>0 are the signal strengths, 𝐮i∈ℝn\mathbf{u}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and 𝐯i∈ℝd\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are left and right singular vectors, and ZZ is the token-specific residual.

The residual ZZ generally exhibits a separable covariance structure (Su and Wu, 2025):

Z=A1/2​X​B1/2,Z=A^{1/2}XB^{1/2}, (15)

where X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} has independent entries, and A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, B∈ℝd×dB\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are deterministic positive-definite matrices describing the temporal dependence across tokens and the coordinate-wise covariance induced by the learned projection weights, respectively. Here B∈ℝd×dB\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is the column covariance matrix as in (Su and Wu, 2025). This colored noise structure is precisely why standard white-noise optimal shrinkage (e.g., Donoho and Gavish (2013)) is insufficient and eOptShrink is needed.

A.2 Key Assumptions

We state the assumptions from (Su and Wu, 2025, Assumption 2.1) adapted to the KV cache setting. Let βd:=n/d\beta_{d}:=n/d denote the aspect ratio and fix a small constant 0<τ<10<\tau<1.

Assumption A.1.

For the model (14)–(15):

  1. (i)

    (Noise entries.) The matrix X=[xi​j]∈ℝn×dX=[x_{ij}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} has independent entries satisfying the bounded support condition with parameter ϕd=d2/a−1/2\phi_{d}=d^{2/a-1/2} for some a>4a>4, and

    maxi,j⁡|𝔼⁡[xi​j]|≤d−2−τ,maxi,j⁡|𝔼⁡[|xi​j|2]−d−1|≤d−2−τ,maxi,j⁡𝔼⁡[|d​xi​j|4]≤C4\max_{i,j}|\mathbb{E}[x_{ij}]|\leq d^{-2-\tau},\quad\max_{i,j}\left|\mathbb{E}[|x_{ij}|^{2}]-d^{-1}\right|\leq d^{-2-\tau},\quad\max_{i,j}\mathbb{E}[|\sqrt{d}\,x_{ij}|^{4}]\leq C_{4}

    for a constant C4>0C_{4}>0. Additionally, the entries have vanishing third moment: 𝔼⁡[xi​j3]=0\mathbb{E}[x_{ij}^{3}]=0 for all i,ji,j. This holds whenever the marginal distributions of xi​jx_{ij} are symmetric about zero, which is a natural condition for centered residual entries.

  2. (ii)

    (Aspect ratio.) τ<n/d<τ−1\tau<n/d<\tau^{-1}.

  3. (iii)

    (Covariance structure.) Denote the eigenvalues of AA as σ1a≥⋯≥σna\sigma_{1}^{a}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{n}^{a} and those of BB as σ1b≥⋯≥σdb\sigma_{1}^{b}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{d}^{b}. We assume

    σ1a∨σ1b≤τ−1andπA​([0,τ])∨πB​([0,τ])≤1−τ.\sigma_{1}^{a}\vee\sigma_{1}^{b}\leq\tau^{-1}\quad\text{and}\quad\pi_{A}([0,\tau])\vee\pi_{B}([0,\tau])\leq 1-\tau.
  4. (iv)

    (Signal strength and effective rank.) The signal strengths satisfy d1≥d2≥⋯≥dr>0d_{1}\geq d_{2}\geq\cdots\geq d_{r}>0 with d1<τ−1d_{1}<\tau^{-1}. Define the critical threshold

    α:=1/𝒯⁡(λ+),\alpha:=1/\sqrt{\mathcal{T}(\lambda_{+})}, (16)

    where λ+\lambda_{+} is the rightmost edge of the noise bulk spectrum and 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the DD-transform defined in (8). There exists an effective rank r+≤rr^{+}\leq r such that dk−α>ϕd+d−1/3d_{k}-\alpha>\phi_{d}+d^{-1/3} if and only if 1≤k≤r+1\leq k\leq r^{+}.

  5. (v)

    (Signal singular vectors.) The left and right singular vectors 𝐮i∈ℝn\mathbf{u}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and 𝐯i∈ℝd\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} of SS are obtained from the QR factorization of independent random matrices with i.i.d. sub-Gaussian entries satisfying the log-Sobolev inequality (Su and Wu, 2025, Assumption 2.1(v)).

Assumptions (i)–(iv) are standard in the spiked random matrix literature (Baik et al., 2005; Yang, 2019; Ding and Yang, 2021). Assumption (v) requires discussion in the KV cache context. Recall that the signal arises from S[t,:]=R(t)⋅h¯tWKS[t,:]=R(t)\cdot\bar{h}_{t}W_{K} and the noise from Z[t,:]=R(t)⋅ϵtWKZ[t,:]=R(t)\cdot\epsilon_{t}W_{K}, where WKW_{K} is the learned (and fixed at inference time) key projection matrix. The local context h¯t\bar{h}_{t} is naturally random: different input sequences produce different local contexts, so the subspace spanned by {h¯t}\{\bar{h}_{t}\} varies across inputs. Since WKW_{K} is deterministic, the signal singular vectors of SS—which are determined by {h¯t​WK}\{\bar{h}_{t}W_{K}\}—inherit their randomness from {h¯t}\{\bar{h}_{t}\} alone. Similarly, the noise ZZ inherits its randomness from the per-token variations ϵt\epsilon_{t} alone. Because h¯t\bar{h}_{t} and ϵt\epsilon_{t} represent independent sources of information (local context versus individual token content), a deterministic linear transformation WKW_{K} applied to both preserves their independence: h¯t​WK⟂ϵt​WK\bar{h}_{t}W_{K}\perp\epsilon_{t}W_{K} follows from h¯t⟂ϵt\bar{h}_{t}\perp\epsilon_{t}, regardless of WKW_{K}. This justifies Assumption (v): the signal singular vectors are random (through {h¯t}\{\bar{h}_{t}\}) and independent of the noise covariance structure (through ϵt\epsilon_{t}). The sub-Gaussian and log-Sobolev conditions on the signal singular vectors are natural for h¯t\bar{h}_{t}, which is a high-dimensional hidden state produced by transformer layers—such representations are well-concentrated in practice.

If one instead conditions on a specific input and treats SS as deterministic, alternative shrinkage frameworks exist: biPCA (Stanley III et al., 2025) handles heteroscedastic noise with deterministic signals, and the whitening-based approaches of Leeb and Romanov (2021); Leeb (2021) provide optimal shrinkage under heteroscedastic or weighted loss settings. However, these methods assume that the noise covariance matrices AA and BB are either known or diagonal, which is not the case for KV cache residuals. eOptShrink avoids this limitation by estimating the noise spectral distribution entirely from the data. As argued in (Su and Wu, 2025, Remark 2.6), when ZZ has an approximately bi-unitarily invariant distribution, the eOptShrink results extend to deterministic signals. We verify empirically (Section 4) that the eOptShrink predictions match observed behavior for the moderate dimensions d=64d=64–128128 encountered in practice.

The threshold α\alpha generalizes the classical BBP phase transition (Baik et al., 2005): signals with di>αd_{i}>\alpha produce outlier singular values that separate from the noise bulk and can be detected, while signals with di≤αd_{i}\leq\alpha are undetectable (their singular values “stick” to λ+\lambda_{+}). Note that α\alpha depends on the full noise covariance structure through AA and BB, not just the variance of ZZ.

Remark A.2 (Symmetry condition).

The stronger eigenvalue sticking bound (19) and isotropic delocalization (21) require either 𝔼⁡[xi​j3]=0\mathbb{E}[x_{ij}^{3}]=0 for all entries, or that AA or BB is diagonal (Su and Wu, 2025; Ding and Yang, 2021, Theorem 3.3, Lemma S.3.13). We use the former: Assumption A.1(i) requires symmetric entry distributions, giving 𝔼⁡[xi​j3]=0\mathbb{E}[x_{ij}^{3}]=0. This is a natural condition for centered residual entries in neural networks and avoids any structural assumption on the covariance matrices AA and BB. Without either condition, weaker bounds hold with additional terms of order ηl≍d−3/4+d−1/2ϕd\eta_{l}\asymp d^{-3/4}+d^{-1/2}\phi_{d} (see (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 3.3)); these suffice for the qualitative conclusions but give less sharp rates.

Remark A.3 (Scope of theoretical guarantees).

Assumption A.1(v) is a modeling assumption: it treats the signal singular vectors as random, which holds when the theory is applied in expectation over input sequences. For a fixed input at inference time, SS is deterministic, and the formal guarantees of Proposition 6.1 and Corollary 6.3 hold as approximations whose quality we verify empirically (Section 4). The practical success of eOptShrink under this gap is consistent with the heuristic argument in (Su and Wu, 2025, Remark 2.6): when ZZ has an approximately bi-unitarily invariant distribution (which holds when XX has i.i.d. entries and AA, BB are generic), the shrinkage estimator is insensitive to whether the signal singular vectors are random or deterministic. We emphasize that eOptShrink’s rank estimation (Step 1 of Algorithm 2), which depends only on the observed eigenvalue distribution and not on the signal structure, is fully justified even for deterministic signals.

A.3 Stochastic Dominance

Following (Su and Wu, 2025), we use the framework of stochastic dominance to state high-probability bounds up to sub-polynomial factors. Let ξ\xi and ζ\zeta be two families of nonnegative random variables indexed by dd (the head dimension, playing the role of the asymptotic parameter). We say ξ\xi is stochastically dominated by ζ\zeta, written ξ≺ζ\xi\prec\zeta, if for any fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and D>0D>0,

ℙ[ξ>dϵζ]≤d−D\mathbb{P}[\xi>d^{\epsilon}\,\zeta]\leq d^{-D} (17)

for all sufficiently large dd. In words, ξ≺ζ\xi\prec\zeta means “ξ\xi is bounded by ζ\zeta with high probability, up to a small power of dd.” We also write ξ=O≺​(ζ)\xi=O_{\prec}(\zeta) interchangeably.

A.4 Singular Value and Vector Behavior

The following results from (Su and Wu, 2025), building on (Donoho et al., 2018; Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi, 2012; Yang, 2019; Ding and Yang, 2021), characterize what happens to the SVD of S~\widetilde{S} relative to the SVD of ZZ. All bounds are stated in terms of stochastic dominance ≺\prec as defined above. We use nn and dd interchangeably as the asymptotic parameter (dd is the column dimension and n=n⁡(d)n=n(d) with n/d→βn/d\to\beta). The notation ϕd:=d2/a−1/2\phi_{d}:=d^{2/a-1/2} for a>4a>4 relates to the moment condition on noise entries, and Δ⁡(di):=|di−α|1/2\Delta(d_{i}):=|d_{i}-\alpha|^{1/2} measures the distance of the ii-th signal strength from the phase transition threshold.

Outlier eigenvalue locations (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 3.2).

For 1≤i≤r+1\leq i\leq r^{+}, the ii-th eigenvalue λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i} of S~​S~⊤\widetilde{S}\widetilde{S}^{\top} satisfies:

|λ~i−θ(di)|≺ϕdΔ(di)2+d−1/2Δ(di),|\tilde{\lambda}_{i}-\theta(d_{i})|\prec\phi_{d}\,\Delta(d_{i})^{2}+d^{-1/2}\Delta(d_{i}), (18)

where θ=𝒯−1\theta=\mathcal{T}^{-1} maps signal strength to the outlier eigenvalue location. This provides a one-to-one correspondence between signal strengths and outlier eigenvalues, with convergence rate controlled by ϕd\phi_{d} and the signal gap Δ⁡(di)\Delta(d_{i}).

Eigenvalue sticking (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 3.3).

For i>r+i>r^{+}, the non-outlier eigenvalues of S~​S~⊤\widetilde{S}\widetilde{S}^{\top} stick to those of Z​Z⊤ZZ^{\top}. Set α+:=min1≤i≤r⁡Δ​(di)2\alpha_{+}:=\min_{1\leq i\leq r}\Delta(d_{i})^{2} and assume α+≥dε(ϕd+d−1/3)\alpha_{+}\geq d^{\varepsilon}(\phi_{d}+d^{-1/3}) for some small ε>0\varepsilon>0. If either 𝔼⁡[xi​j3]=0\mathbb{E}[x_{ij}^{3}]=0 for all i,ji,j, or AA or BB is diagonal, then:

|λ~r++i−λi|≺1d​α+for ​1≤i≤τ​d,|\tilde{\lambda}_{r^{+}+i}-\lambda_{i}|\prec\frac{1}{d\,\alpha_{+}}\quad\text{for }1\leq i\leq\tau d, (19)

where λi\lambda_{i} are the eigenvalues of Z​Z⊤ZZ^{\top}. This is crucial: after removing the top r+r^{+} components, the residual’s spectrum matches the pure noise spectrum up to O≺​(1/(d​α+))O_{\prec}(1/(d\,\alpha_{+})).

Delocalization of non-outlier singular vectors (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 3.4).

For r++1≤i≤c​dr^{+}+1\leq i\leq cd and j=1,…,rj=1,\ldots,r, the non-outlier singular vectors 𝝃~i,𝜻~i\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i},\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i} of S~\widetilde{S} satisfy:

|⟨𝐮j,𝝃~i⟩|2∨|⟨𝐯j,𝜻~i⟩|2≺d−1+ϕd3Δ​(dj)4+ϕd2+ϰi,|\langle\mathbf{u}_{j},\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\rangle|^{2}\vee|\langle\mathbf{v}_{j},\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}\rangle|^{2}\prec\frac{d^{-1}+\phi_{d}^{3}}{\Delta(d_{j})^{4}+\phi_{d}^{2}+\varkappa_{i}}, (20)

where ϰi:=i2/3d−2/3\varkappa_{i}:=i^{2/3}d^{-2/3}. When signals are well-separated from the threshold (dj−α≳1d_{j}-\alpha\gtrsim 1), this gives |⟨𝐮j,𝝃~i⟩|2≺d−1|\langle\mathbf{u}_{j},\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\rangle|^{2}\prec d^{-1}—the non-outlier singular vectors are delocalized and carry no signal information. This is the key property ensuring the residual has no preferred directions after signal removal.

Isotropic delocalization of noise eigenvectors (Ding and Yang, 2021, Lemma S.3.13).

The eigenvectors of the pure noise matrix Z=A1/2​X​B1/2Z=A^{1/2}XB^{1/2} satisfy a stronger, coordinate-wise delocalization. Let 𝝃k\bm{\xi}_{k} and 𝜻k\bm{\zeta}_{k} denote the left and right singular vectors of ZZ. If either 𝔼⁡[xi​j3]=0\mathbb{E}[x_{ij}^{3}]=0 for all i,ji,j, or AA or BB is diagonal, then for any deterministic unit vectors 𝐮∈ℝn\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and 𝐯∈ℝd\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and all kk with eigenvalue γk\gamma_{k} near the bulk edge λ+\lambda_{+}:

|⟨𝐮,𝝃k⟩|2+|⟨𝐯,𝜻k⟩|2≺d−1.|\langle\mathbf{u},\bm{\xi}_{k}\rangle|^{2}+|\langle\mathbf{v},\bm{\zeta}_{k}\rangle|^{2}\prec d^{-1}. (21)

In particular, choosing 𝐯=ej\mathbf{v}=e_{j} (the jj-th standard basis vector in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}) gives |𝜻k​(j)|2≺d−1|\bm{\zeta}_{k}(j)|^{2}\prec d^{-1} for all coordinates jj—no coordinate of the noise eigenvectors carries disproportionate energy. Combined with the eigenvalue sticking (19), this extends to the non-outlier singular vectors of S~\widetilde{S}: the residual’s right singular vectors are delocalized not only with respect to the signal directions (Eq. (20)) but also with respect to the standard coordinate basis. This is the key property underlying Corollary 6.3: the rows of the residual RR, when normalized, are approximately uniform on the sphere 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1}, satisfying the precondition for TurboQuant’s near-optimal quantization (Zandieh et al., 2025, Lemma 1).

Optimal shrinker convergence (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 4.4).

Let c∈(0,1/2)c\in(0,1/2), and assume the conditions of Theorem 3.3 hold with dε(ϕd+d−1/3)>d−1/6d^{\varepsilon}(\phi_{d}+d^{-1/3})>d^{-1/6}. Then for 1≤i≤r^+1\leq i\leq\hat{r}^{+}, conditional on the event {r^+=r+}\{\hat{r}^{+}=r^{+}\} (which holds with high probability by (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 4.2)), the eOptShrink estimator satisfies:

|φi∗−φ^e,i|≺ϕd+d−1/2/Δ(di)|\varphi^{*}_{i}-\hat{\varphi}_{e,i}|\prec\phi_{d}+d^{-1/2}/\Delta(d_{i}) (22)

for all three loss functions (Frobenius, operator, nuclear norm). In particular, |φ∗i−φ^e,i|≤d−1/2+ϵ|\varphi^{*}_{i}-\hat{\varphi}_{e,i}|\leq d^{-1/2+\epsilon} with high probability for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

A.5 The eOptShrink Algorithm

The eOptShrink algorithm is presented in Algorithm 2 (Section 2.3). The key innovation over OptShrink (Nadakuditi, 2014) is that it does not require knowledge of the rank or the noise covariance structure. The rank is estimated automatically via the bulk edge (Step 1), and the noise spectral distribution is recovered by imputing the eigenvalues perturbed by signals (Step 2), exploiting the eigenvalue sticking property (19).

A.6 Proof of Proposition 6.1

Proof.

We prove each part in turn. Throughout, we condition on the high-probability event {r^+=r+}\{\hat{r}^{+}=r^{+}\}, which holds by (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 4.2).

Part 1. The eOptShrink estimate is S^=∑i=1r+φ^e,i​𝝃~i​𝜻~i⊤\hat{S}=\sum_{i=1}^{r^{+}}\hat{\varphi}_{e,i}\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}^{\top}. Writing S~=∑i=1n∧dσ~i​𝝃~i​𝜻~i⊤\widetilde{S}=\sum_{i=1}^{n\wedge d}\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}^{\top}, the residual decomposes as

R=S~−S^=∑i=1r+(σ~i−φ^e,i)​𝝃~i​𝜻~i⊤+∑i=r++1n∧dσ~i​𝝃~i​𝜻~i⊤.R=\widetilde{S}-\hat{S}=\sum_{i=1}^{r^{+}}(\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}-\hat{\varphi}_{e,i})\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}^{\top}+\sum_{i=r^{+}+1}^{n\wedge d}\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}^{\top}. (23)

We analyze the two sums separately.

Outlier components (1≤i≤r+1\leq i\leq r^{+}). By the optimal shrinker convergence (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 4.4), |φ^e,i−φi∗|≺ϕd+d−1/2/Δ(di)|\hat{\varphi}_{e,i}-\varphi^{*}_{i}|\prec\phi_{d}+d^{-1/2}/\Delta(d_{i}). The Frobenius-optimal shrinker satisfies φi∗=di​a1,i​a2,i\varphi^{*}_{i}=d_{i}\sqrt{a_{1,i}a_{2,i}}, where a1,ia_{1,i} and a2,ia_{2,i} are the asymptotic squared inner products between the clean and noisy singular vectors (Su and Wu, 2025, Proposition 2.1). By the outlier eigenvalue location (18), σ~i2=θ(di)+O≺(ϕdΔ(di)2+d−1/2Δ(di))\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}^{2}=\theta(d_{i})+O_{\prec}(\phi_{d}\Delta(d_{i})^{2}+d^{-1/2}\Delta(d_{i})), where θ⁡(di)=𝒯−1​(di−2)\theta(d_{i})=\mathcal{T}^{-1}(d_{i}^{-2}) encodes both the signal strength did_{i} and the noise bias. The optimal shrinker φi∗\varphi^{*}_{i} is constructed to satisfy (φi∗)2=di2​a1,i​a2,i(\varphi^{*}_{i})^{2}=d_{i}^{2}a_{1,i}a_{2,i}, so that the Frobenius-norm contribution of the ii-th component in S^\hat{S} matches the signal energy in that direction. The residual singular value is therefore

σ~i−φ^e,i=(σ~i−φi∗)+O≺(ϕd+d−1/2/Δ(di)).\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}-\hat{\varphi}_{e,i}=(\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}-\varphi^{*}_{i})+O_{\prec}(\phi_{d}+d^{-1/2}/\Delta(d_{i})).

To show this does not separate from the bulk, note that σ~i=θ⁡(di)+O≺(ϕd+d−1/2)\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}=\sqrt{\theta(d_{i})}+O_{\prec}(\phi_{d}+d^{-1/2}) by (18), where θ⁡(di)>λ+\sqrt{\theta(d_{i})}>\sqrt{\lambda_{+}} is the outlier location. The shrinker φi∗\varphi^{*}_{i} is chosen so that σ~i−φi∗\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}-\varphi^{*}_{i} equals the noise-only singular value that would appear in the ii-th direction if the signal were absent. Since the noise singular values are bounded by λ++O≺(d−2/3)\sqrt{\lambda_{+}}+O_{\prec}(d^{-2/3}) (the Tracy–Widom edge fluctuation), we have |σ~i−φ^e,i|≤λ++O≺(d−2/3+ϕd)|\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}-\hat{\varphi}_{e,i}|\leq\sqrt{\lambda_{+}}+O_{\prec}(d^{-2/3}+\phi_{d}), which lies within the bulk.

Non-outlier components (i>r+i>r^{+}). By the eigenvalue sticking theorem (19), |λ~r++i−λi|≺1/(d​α+)|\tilde{\lambda}_{r^{+}+i}-\lambda_{i}|\prec 1/(d\,\alpha_{+}) for 1≤i≤τ​d1\leq i\leq\tau d, where λi\lambda_{i} are the eigenvalues of Z​Z⊤ZZ^{\top}. By the delocalization theorem (20), |⟨𝐮j,𝝃~r++i⟩|2≺(d−1+ϕd3)/(Δ​(dj)4+ϕd2+ϰi)|\langle\mathbf{u}_{j},\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{r^{+}+i}\rangle|^{2}\prec(d^{-1}+\phi_{d}^{3})/(\Delta(d_{j})^{4}+\phi_{d}^{2}+\varkappa_{i}), so the non-outlier singular vectors of S~\widetilde{S} are O≺​(d−1)O_{\prec}(d^{-1})-orthogonal to all signal directions when dj−α≳1d_{j}-\alpha\gtrsim 1. These components therefore carry no signal energy and their eigenvalues match those of Z​Z⊤ZZ^{\top}. Combined with the analysis of the outlier components, the empirical spectral distribution of R​R⊤RR^{\top} converges to that of Z​Z⊤ZZ^{\top}.

Part 2. Write R=S~−S^=(S−S^)+ZR=\widetilde{S}-\hat{S}=(S-\hat{S})+Z. Expanding the squared Frobenius norm:

‖R‖F2=‖S−S^‖F2+‖Z‖F2+2​⟨S−S^,Z⟩F.\left\lVert R\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\left\lVert S-\hat{S}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\left\lVert Z\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+2\langle S-\hat{S},Z\rangle_{F}. (24)

Remark A.4.

The constant c=min⁡(1/2.01, 1/log⁡log⁡d)c=\min(1/2.01,\,1/\log\log d) in Algorithm 2 balances two requirements: k=⌊dc⌋k=\lfloor d^{c}\rfloor must be large enough that k≫r+k\gg r^{+} (so the bulk edge estimate is not contaminated by outliers) and small enough that the imputed eigenvalues remain close to the true edge (requiring c<1/2c<1/2 for the convergence guarantees in (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorems 4.1–4.4)). For KV cache blocks with d=64d=64–128128, this gives k≈7k\approx 7–1111, which suffices since the typical effective rank is r+≈1r^{+}\approx 1–55.

Proof.

We condition on the high-probability event {r^+=r+}\{\hat{r}^{+}=r^{+}\} throughout. The residual decomposes via the SVD of S~\widetilde{S} as in (23):

We bound the jj-th coordinate of the tt-th row for each part separately.

Step 1: Outlier contribution.

By the isotropic delocalization of the outlier singular vectors (Su and Wu, 2025, Theorem 3.4) applied with 𝐯=ej\mathbf{v}=e_{j}, we have |𝜻~i​(j)|2≺d−1|\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}(j)|^{2}\prec d^{-1} for each jj and 1≤i≤r+1\leq i\leq r^{+} (since the outlier right singular vectors, while aligned with the signal directions 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i}, are still unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and their coordinates satisfy |𝜻~i​(j)|2=|a2,i​𝐯i​(j)+noise|2|\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}(j)|^{2}=|a_{2,i}\mathbf{v}_{i}(j)+\text{noise}|^{2}, where 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i} has delocalized coordinates by Assumption A.1(v) and a2,i<1a_{2,i}<1). Rbulk​(t,j)=∑i=r++1n∧dσ~i​𝝃~i​(t)​𝜻~i​(j)=et⊤​Rbulk​ej.R_{\text{bulk}}(t,j)=\sum_{i=r^{+}+1}^{n\wedge d}\widetilde{\sigma}_{i}\,\tilde{\bm{\xi}}_{i}(t)\,\tilde{\bm{\zeta}}_{i}(j)=e_{t}^{\top}R_{\text{bulk}}\,e_{j}.

The total coordinate is rt​(j)=Rout​(t,j)+Rbulk​(t,j)r_{t}(j)=R_{\text{out}}(t,j)+R_{\text{bulk}}(t,j). From Step 1, |Rout​(t,j)|2≺r+​λ+/(n​d)=O⁡(1/n)|R_{\text{out}}(t,j)|^{2}\prec r^{+}\lambda_{+}/(nd)=O(1/n). From Step 2, |Rbulk​(t,j)|2≺1|R_{\text{bulk}}(t,j)|^{2}\prec 1. Since ‖rt‖22=Θ⁡(d)\|r_{t}\|_{2}^{2}=\Theta(d), the dominant contribution is from the bulk, and For each fixed jj, we have |rt​(j)|2/‖rt‖22≺d−1|r_{t}(j)|^{2}/\|r_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\prec d^{-1}. Taking the maximum over j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d via a union bound:

ℙ[max1≤j≤d|rt​(j)|2‖rt‖22>C2log⁡dd]≤∑j=1dℙ[|rt​(j)|2‖rt‖22>C2log⁡dd]≤d⋅d−D\mathbb{P}\!\left[\max_{1\leq j\leq d}\frac{|r_{t}(j)|^{2}}{\|r_{t}\|_{2}^{2}}>C^{2}\frac{\log d}{d}\right]\leq\sum_{j=1}^{d}\mathbb{P}\!\left[\frac{|r_{t}(j)|^{2}}{\|r_{t}\|_{2}^{2}}>C^{2}\frac{\log d}{d}\right]\leq d\cdot d^{-D}

for any D>0D>0 and sufficiently large CC (by the ≺\prec bound). Choosing D>1D>1 gives the result with high probability. Taking square roots yields (13). ∎
